 Warning: This post contains major spoilers for Season 1 of Carrie 
 Carrie White may have survived her bloody prom night , but she'd better keep an eye on the horizon for future dangers. In a major departure from Stephen King canon, Mike Flanagan 's eight-episode Prime Video adaptation of the author's classic 1974 novel, Carrie , ends with the titular telekinesis-powered teen (played by Summer H. Howell ) alive and kinda well after she wreaked havoc on the small town of Chamberlain, Maine. 
 Now we know why; the streamer recently announced that the series will return for a second season , something that Flanagan was only able to hint at when Gold Derby spoke with him earlier this month. "My dream scenario is a three-step arc for Carrie that I'd be so excited to explore," Flanagan teases. "But our priority was to make sure this season could stand alone as well as it possibly could."
 Related Stories The ‘Carrie’ crafts team takes you inside the show’s blood-drenched prom Mike Flanagan’s ‘Carrie’ to submit in drama categories at awards shows following cliffhanger ending and Season 2 pickup 
 While he couldn't confirm a Season 2 at the time of our conversation, Flanagan does stress that his version of Carrie's story always ended with her still alive, and not in the fake-out dream sequence way that served as the final jump scare in Brian De Palma 's much-loved 1976 movie version. "Especially in a show for young people, I could not in good conscience give them a hopeless story — not with the way the world is," he emphasizes. "I mean, if we, as adults, don't have any hope to offer them, we might as well just hang this up."
 Not for nothing, but Flanagan does reference the novel and film's original ending in the closing moments of the Season 1 finale. After destroying her house and killing her mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan) — or so she thinks, anyway — Carrie imagines herself lying next to her deceased dad (Tahmoh Penikett, one of many Battlestar Galactica alums that Flanagan recruited for the series ) while awaiting her own death. But then her seemingly imaginary, but actually very real friend Emaline (Thalia Dudek) rides to her rescue. In a direct echo of De Palma's movie, Carrie raises her hand out of her grave — and Emaline grasps it. 
 "I'm so glad you spotted that shot," Flanagan says, confirming the 50-years-later homage. "It felt critical to me that this version of the story end on a note of hope without diminishing any of the tragedy. And Carrie will have to reckon with that on the other side of this ending." 
 Naturally, we had some burning questions about what's waiting on the other side of the fiery finale, as well as lingering mysteries from Season 1. And Flanagan was game to answer as much as he could — lest he attract Randall Flagg's wrath. 
 Why did the Carrie title card change from white to red during the course of the series? 
 The way the title cards in #Carrie get bloodier with every episode is such a brilliant detail. You can literally watch the horror creeping in without a single word being said. pic.twitter.com/AjjD2IhHBX 
— WATCHER (@Harsikomide) October 12, 2026 
 "That was a fun idea we had as we went into post," Flanagan said of a detail that several eagle-eyed viewers — including Gold Derby — noticed. "We were playing with our various title options, and as the show changed and Carrie's journey changed, we were driving from this kind of innocence toward blood. I'm glad you picked that up. A lot of people haven't spotted that, but yeah, it's just a subtle little way to help support her arc."
 How many times did that bucket of blood drop?
 View this post on Instagram 
 Taking a literal bloodbath just comes with the territory when you're tasked with playing Carrie White — going all the way back to the O.G. Carrie, Sissy Spacek . In a 2018 interview, the star of De Palma's film said that she was doused in pig's blood twice while shooting the final scene, and described it as feeling like a "warm blanket."
 "Don't tell Summer that," Flanagan jokes when informed of Spacek's recollection. "We did four blood drops on her over the course of three days — and it didn't feel like a warm blanket! It felt very cold, very sticky, and very heavy." And the writer-director owns up to the fact that there was an extra drop that resulted in a blown take. "We needed to shoot it with a wide perspective, but the problem was that the further back our cameras were, the easier it was to only hit the back of Summer's neck or the top of her head with the blood," he recalls. "On one take, all we did was knock her tiara off, which meant we couldn't use it and had to clean her up and do it again, which was a two-hour process.
 "She went through an awful lot," Flanagan says admiringly of his star. "I remember watching her try to use her phone or eat, and she couldn't because of all the sticky blood. And anytime she'd sit in a chair, she'd leave this giant blood print on it when she stood up, so we'd have to put these big pieces of plastic on the chairs and peel them off afterward."
 Flanagan also says that he made a conscious decision not to ape De Palma's film by using slow motion or multiple camera angles for Carrie's final humiliation, instead presenting it as a short, sharp shock. "I really liked that idea of falling off a cliff from adulation into utter silence," he says, adding that Howell made the choice for Carrie to essentially go catatonic after the blood drop instead of reacting with horror in the same way that Spacek did. 
 "Summer told me, 'I would freeze and collapse into myself,'" Flanagan says. "And I think that's such a great choice; there's this moment where she shuts her eyes and tries to leave her body, but there's nowhere else to go. That came from Summer deciding what her version of Carrie would do." 
 Did Carrie or Emaline kill Tommy Ross?
 Howell and Joel Oulette in 'Carrie' Prime Video 
 Carrie may not be able to escape her body in that moment, but she does surrender control of it to Emaline, who at that point is still an astral projection. "Let me take the wheel, OK?" the more experienced telekinetic says as the prom descends into full chaos. Asked whether Emaline potentially "helped" her friend before that exchange — either by blowing up the phones of every kid in that gym, showering them with glass, or pulling down the catwalk that killed her prom date, Tommy — Flanagan confirms that's all Carrie's unleashed rage.
 "It's Carrie who kills Tommy, even though it's an accident," he says. "It's also Carrie who explodes everyone's phones — that detail was very important to me. But we also wanted to make the culpability of the prom complicated, because there had to be something left of Carrie emotionally after this experience if we were going to let the character live. Audiences can forgive an antihero, but we are talking about killing dozens of kids and that's harder for them — and Carrie — to come back from."
 But Carrie does consciously kill two of those kids, and not by accident. "Emaline is standing off to the side when Carrie kills Chris and Billy," Flanagan notes, referring to the bullies that are responsible for her blood bath. "She walks right up to them, looks Chris in the eye, and crushes her to death. There's nobody else to blame."
 Is Emaline from the Firestarter Initiative? 
 Thalia Dudek in 'Carrie' Prime Video 
 Aside from Carrie living to fight — and maybe kill? — another day, Flanagan's other major revision to King's text was adding an entire secret society of "gifted women" like Emaline who descend on Chamberlain as Carrie's powers reveal themselves. "In the writer's room, we talked about how they'd need to send a spy, and we loved the idea of accomplishing that via astral projection," he explains. "But we also knew that if we had an astral projection that didn't interact with anyone else or touch anything, the audience would figure it out quickly. They've been trained by Fight Club and The Sixth Sense to look for that kind of stuff." 
 So Flanagan decided to short circuit the guessing game by revealing midway through the season that Emaline may be a figment of Carrie's imagination. The character promptly disappeared for an entire episode, but then appeared in the finale, first as an astral projection and then as a physical presence in the final moments of the finale. "As writers, we liked the idea that the reason Emaline wasn't there for an entire episode is because she was in a car on the way to Chamberlain," Flanagan says with a smile. "It was a great way to do a double twist, but one that made perfect sense with the story we were telling."
 Expect to learn more about the secret society that Emaline belongs to in Season 2, but Flanagan neatly dodges our semi-joking question about whether it involves the "Firestarter Initiative," aka The Shop, the government agency that turned Charlie McGee into the young pyrokinetic at the center of King's 1980 novel Firestarter . "We've hinted at the wider world that Carrie's headed off into, and that's her fate," he says carefully. "She's earned that ending, whether he follow her or not. If she leaves us on the road and drives off into the horizon, that's OK for me, too."
 Is there a Dark Tower on the horizon?
 Howell as Carrie White Prime Video 
 The view that Carrie and Emaline see through their front windshield as Chamberlain recedes in the rearview is notably absent the towering nexus point that binds the larger King-verse together, and forms the basis for his much-loved Dark Tower books. Flanagan has been working with Prime Video to turn those novels into a TV series for some time now, but we're not any closer to any Gunslinger or Crimson King sightings and he promises that Carrie isn't a backdoor pilot for that show. Still, the King fan in him couldn't resist a shout-out or two.
 " Dark Tower fans are going to love the signage at the place where Ralph White works," Flanagan says, calling out the fact that Carrie's dad works for LeMerk Industries, which is a known ally of the Crimson King. "But we tried to keep that kind of stuff in the background."
 Informed that we were scanning the background for some l ow men — or low girls — in yellow coats , Flanagan appreciatively laughs at the reference to that Dark Tower -connected novella included in King's 1999 anthology, Hearts in Atlantis , and served as the basis for a 2001 movie starring Anthony Hopkins. "That's one of my favorite books of his," he says. "I would love to take a crack at adapting it, because the other movie only did one-fifth of it. All of the stories in Hearts in Atlantis are so gorgeously connected, and the fact that it touches the Dark Tower is even better." 
 Where was Dick Hallorann? 
 Samantha Sloyan in 'Carrie' Prime Video 
 Pour one out for Margaret White, who does die at the end of Flanagan's Carrie , but not by her daughter's hand. Instead, she's executed by the writer-director's wife, Kate Siegel, who plays Adelaide, another gifted woman pursuing Carrie. Before killing Margaret, though, Adelaide tells her that her powers come from " the Shine ," the term that King first dropped in his 1977 horror classic The Shining and has since spread throughout the larger King-verse.
 "I honest believe that if Carrie had been written just a few books later, it probably would have been called The Shining ," Flanagan says. King himself allowed that book's characters to wander into other stories; for example, the Overlook Hotel's Shining-enabled chef Dick Hallorann, also appeared in the backstory of It — an inclusion that was reflected in the recent HBO prequel series, It: Welcome to Derry . But Flanagan resisted the impulse to place an older version of Dick in the Chamberlain High cafeteria.
 "We already have Castle Rock that functions as the King anthology series," he notes, referring to the Hulu series that ran for two seasons. "That was a really fun experiment in putting all of these Stephen King things together, but I wanted to focus this show on Carrie White and the larger sorority of women around her."
 But Flanagan allows that could change as Season 2 of Carrie goes from being theoretical to being reality. "There's so much possibility for ways other characters and other connections could materialize," he teases. "That would come down to conversations with Stephen, and which of his characters he would be interested in seeing interact in this new strange sandbox we've made out of Carrie ."
 — Additional reporting by Marcus James Dixon
